title: Pawn weaknesses

D0.outcome: Names isolated, doubled, backward and passed pawns in a position and says why each can be a weakness or a strength.

D1.outcome: Marks each pawn's type and the squares and pieces that make it a target.

D2.outcome: In unlabeled positions, rates a pawn as a real weakness, harmless, or compensated, and chooses the plan; applies the stop-square condition for a backward pawn.

D3.outcome: Predicts how one feature (a neighbouring pawn, an open file, the bishop pair, the phase of the game) flips the verdict, and fixes then out-counts a backward pawn.

misconceptions: A weakness is a weakness in every phase.
Every pawn behind its neighbours is backward and a target.
conditions: A backward pawn is a target when it cannot advance (the stop square is controlled), lies on a semi-open file, and the attacker's pieces have access.
Whether doubled or isolated pawns weaken depends on phase and piece activity; the bishop pair or an open file can compensate.
contrasts: A backward pawn that can advance safely, or whose stop square the opponent cannot reach, is not a target.
Backward pawns and holes 'invariably lead to disaster' (absolute wording; Sicilian and Hedgehog structures live with them).
The same weakness on a file the attacker cannot reach.

soft_prereq_notes.POS.PASSED.D1: the passed pawn is the opposite of a weakness
